I dwell on how the event could have been prevented

Memory.value: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop

There is something wrong with me as a person

issues.item: Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
issues.explanation: For intimate partner physical abuse, 'being forced to do something' and tactile body-state cues are plausible triggers, but 'burnt smell' introduces a danger cue more typical of fire/explosion trauma and is not supported by the other selected items. It feels disconnected from the stated trauma and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The appraisal pattern is otherwise self-blaming/defectiveness-focused and tightly linked to triggers, but 'fear of rage' shifts to fear of one's own future violent loss of control. That theme is not supported by the trauma type, the other appraisals, or the maladaptive strategies, making this item difficult to integrate into the same formulation.

issues.item: Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time; Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
issues.explanation: The memory items indicate highly severe, here-and-now re-experiencing, which is plausible at this PCL-5 level, but they sit awkwardly with the formulation because Memory has only a weak link to Negative Appraisals and no active links to Triggers or Maladaptive Strategies. Selecting two very strong reliving items plus disorganized narration makes Memory appear more central than the formulation suggests.

vignette:
Mai is a 35-year-old Vietnamese American physical therapist who came to treatment after months of telling herself that what happened was over and that she should be able to get on with her life. She is married now, but the trauma she described began in a previous romantic relationship marked by escalating physical abuse. In the sessions, when she approached the memory directly, her account repeatedly broke apart. She would begin with an ordinary detail-the apartment, the argument, the feeling that she needed to leave-and then lose the thread, stop mid-sentence, and press her hands together as if bracing herself. What did come through clearly was the bodily immediacy of the abuse. She remembered being grabbed and overpowered when she tried to pull away, the shock of physical touch turning instantly from familiar to dangerous, and the feeling of being forced into stillness while her own wishes no longer mattered. She also remembered the temperature on her skin with disturbing vividness: the cold surface against her arm and the abrupt contrast of air on her body during the assault. Those sensations remained lodged in her memory in a way that felt more alive than narrative, so that later a certain chill on her skin could bring the whole scene back with a force that made it seem not remembered but current.

In the weeks after leaving that relationship, Mai had expected fear and anger, but what took hold most strongly was humiliation. She had come to believe that the abuse exposed something defective in her, something about the way she acted that had made it happen. She did not say this abstractly; she said it as if it were settled fact. If she had not said certain things, if she had noticed the signs earlier, if she had not stayed as long as she did, then maybe none of it would have happened. She spent long stretches mentally revisiting moments before the assaults, trying to identify the exact point at which she should have acted differently. At other times she found herself dwelling on the version of herself from before the abuse-more relaxed, more open, less watchful. She spoke about that earlier self almost as if she were talking about another woman she had lost.

These experiences became woven into her daily life at work. As a physical therapist, Mai spends her days in close proximity to patients, guiding movement, applying manual support, and being touched in return as part of routine care. That setting repeatedly confronted her with the very sensations she feared. A patient's hand reaching suddenly toward her forearm, even in a benign and expected way, could make her whole body tense. The coolness of a treatment room, or a draft of air across exposed skin while adjusting a patient's position, could stop her for a moment with the feeling that she was back in the apartment. When this happened, the memory did not arrive to her as a story from the past. It happened all at once, with such emotional force that she had to fight to remain in the room. On several occasions she excused herself abruptly, went into a supply area, and waited for the wave of panic and shame to pass. She could not explain to colleagues why she seemed suddenly distant or flustered, and the inability to put what happened into words deepened her sense that something was wrong with her.

Outside work, she became sharply vigilant around other people, especially men whose tone, posture, or nearness felt even vaguely controlling. In ordinary interactions she scanned for who might be dangerous, where the exits were, whether someone might block her path or insist on something she did not want. Situations that involved pressure or expectation became especially charged. What frightened her most was the feeling of losing autonomy again, so even minor moments-someone standing too close, someone insisting she do something quickly, even affectionate touch she had not initiated-could flood her with alarm and anger that seemed to arrive before thought. At home this strained her marriage. Her husband was described as caring and patient, but Mai found herself recoiling from touch she had once welcomed, then feeling ashamed for doing so. She wanted closeness and at the same time felt compelled to protect herself from it.

By the time she sought help, the cost had become harder to ignore. She was exhausted by how much of her mental life was spent looking backward-either to the abuse itself or to the person she believed she had been before it. She was tired of rehearsing how it could have been prevented, tired of being ambushed by cold air or casual contact in the clinic, tired of starting to tell the story and feeling her mind scatter under the weight of it. What finally brought her in was a recent moment at work when a patient gripped her wrist unexpectedly during an exercise and she froze so completely that another therapist had to step in. Mai left that day convinced she was unraveling. She came to treatment afraid that the humiliation had marked her permanently and that there was something fundamentally damaged in her, but also hoping, cautiously, that she might one day be able to feel present in her own life again rather than perpetually pulled back into what happened.
